traveler: Felipe Guamán Poma de Ayala (Waman Puma)
title: The Letter That Never Arrived: an Andean lord walks Peru to write to the King of Spain
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Cajamarca, the capture that precedes him
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1533 as carried in pizarro.journey.json, from which this pin is inherited byte for byte; the father's later action against Hernández Girón is attested in the manuscript at pp. 434-435 without a year
stops.campa: In the plaza of Cajamarca, Francisco Pizarro takes the Inca Atahualpa alive, and the empire that ordered the roads and the storehouses passes in an afternoon to a company of one hundred and sixty-eight Spaniards. Guamán Poma is not yet born, or is an infant in Lucanas. He will draw this scene. His father, Martín Guamán Malqui, will fight for the crown against the rebel encomendero Francisco Hernández Girón at Uata Cocha, one hundred of his men against three hundred, and the chronicle records it as service the crown never repaid.
suggested_refs: Drawing 174 of the Nueva corónica, the father at Uata Cocha, poma.kb.dk pp. 434-435
sources: pizarro.journey.json
Royal Danish Library, poma.kb.dk, ch. 19, pp. 434-435, Drawing 174
English Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'

stops.name: Sondondo, the birth without a date
stops.date_confidence: contested: c.1534 per the Spanish account, c.1535 per the English, and as late as c.1550 in some scholarship; no baptismal or civil record survives, and the village San Cristóbal de Suntuntu does not survive as a fixed colonial toponym, so the coordinate is the Sondondo valley seat in Cabana district
stops.campa: In the terraced valley of Sondondo, in the province of Lucanas, a son is born to don Martín Guamán Malqui de Ayala and doña Juana Curi Ocllo. He gives the year nowhere in the thousand pages he will write, and no baptismal book survives to supply it; scholars set his birth anywhere between 1534 and 1550. The village he names, San Cristóbal de Suntuntu, has no fixed colonial location, so his birthplace is inferred from the valley communities he keeps calling his patria. He is born into a country two years conquered.
suggested_refs: The terraced hillsides of the Sondondo valley, Cabana district, Lucanas, Ayacucho
sources: Royal Danish Library, El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno, GKS 2232 4to (poma.kb.dk), p. 15
Rolena Adorno, Guaman Poma: Writing and Resistance in Colonial Peru (1986)
English and Spanish Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'
GeoNames, Sondondo and Cabana, Lucanas

stops.name: Huánuco Pampa, the lineage claimed
stops.date_confidence: no date: the Yarovilca descent is a pre-Hispanic claim entered in the manuscript, and the nominal year here only fixes the pin in his lifetime; no colonial document corroborates the genealogy and nothing places him at this site
stops.campa: Far to the north, on the puna above the Vizcarra, the ushnu platform and the great storehouses of Huánuco Pampa stand as the seat of the Yarovilca lords. Guamán Poma traces his father's line to them, and through his mother to Inca blood, and signs himself descendant of Huaman Chava Ayauca Yarovilca Huánuco. No colonial document corroborates the genealogy; it survives in his own testimony and in the petitions he files upon it. The name itself is the claim: waman, the falcon; puma, the lion of the Andes.
stops.quote: Uira Cocha Runa, Uari Runa, que desendio de Noe del diluuio, Uari Runa, y de Puron Runa y de Auca Runa
stops.quote_source: Nueva corónica y buen gobierno, Letter to King Philip III (f. 9), transcription at poma.kb.dk
suggested_refs: The ushnu platform and qollqa storehouses of Huánuco Pampa, near La Unión, Dos de Mayo
sources: Nueva corónica y buen gobierno (self-attestation), poma.kb.dk
English Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'
John Murra, introductory studies on Waman Puma
GeoNames, Pampa Huánuco Viejo

stops.name: Sondondo, the house of Martín Guamán Malqui
stops.date_confidence: no dated record of the childhood exists; the household, the parents' names and the half-brother are attested only in the manuscript itself, and the year here is a nominal placement of his schooling
stops.campa: In the house at Sondondo the boy learns Quechua from his mother and the letters from his half-brother, whom the chronicle names Father Martín de Ayala, a mestizo priest and, in his account, a great and holy man who teaches him Christian doctrine and to read. The father is a curaca who served the crown; the brother says mass. The book that comes out of this house will be written in both tongues at once, Spanish braided with Quechua and Aymara, in an orthography no schoolmaster ever corrected. A priest teaches him to read, and he will spend his life accusing priests.
suggested_refs: The chapter on the author's father and on Father Martín de Ayala, poma.kb.dk pp. 749-751
sources: Royal Danish Library, poma.kb.dk, pp. 15 and 749-751
English Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'

stops.name: Huamanga province, riding with Albornoz
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline, loose in date: the Spanish account places Cristóbal de Albornoz in Huamanga 1569-1571, while the broader Taki Onqoy campaign runs from c.1564; the coordinate stands for the village circuit, not one settlement
stops.campa: The huacas are speaking again. The movement the Spanish call Taki Onqoy, the dancing sickness, teaches that the old shrines will rise and throw down the Christian god, and Cristóbal de Albornoz, secular priest and ecclesiastical visitador, rides the villages of Huamanga to break it: shrines smashed, dancers whipped, hair cut off. Guamán Poma rides with him as the tongue, turning the accusation into Quechua and the answer back into Spanish. This is his apprenticeship in what a visita is, and in what one does to a village.
suggested_refs: Albornoz's Taki Onqoy visita records for the Huamanga villages
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'
Spanish Wikipedia, 'Cristóbal de Albornoz'
Kenneth Mills, Idolatry and Its Enemies (2004)
Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)

stops.name: Parinacochas, the campaign turns south
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the extension of Albornoz's visita into Parinacochas is drawn from the campaign's documented scope rather than from any paper naming Guamán Poma in this province
stops.campa: The campaign runs south into Parinacochas, and the same work is done in the same order: the shrine located, the dancers named, the sentence read aloud in a language the punished do not speak and the interpreter supplies. He hears every word of it twice. Forty years later the chronicle will spend chapter after chapter on what parish priests do to indigenous parishioners, and the detail in those chapters is the detail of a man who stood at the priest's elbow and said it for him, village by village, in the words the priest chose.
suggested_refs: The Parinacochas lagoon and the villages of its basin, southern edge of the Albornoz circuit
sources: Kenneth Mills, Idolatry and Its Enemies (2004)
Rolena Adorno on the scope of Albornoz's visita

stops.name: Huamanga, interpreter to the Advocate General of the Indians
stops.date_confidence: attested service, undated: the Spanish account names Alberto de Acuña, known as the Advocate General of the Indians, and places the work loosely in the 1560s and 1570s without a year; it gives him no judicial title, and the earlier description of him as an oidor is unsupported
stops.campa: He works as interpreter for Alberto de Acuña, known as the Advocate General of the Indians, the office charged with putting native litigants' claims before colonial courts. The record gives the service and not the year. He is by now a professional intermediary, useful to extirpators and to advocates alike and paid by both, a man who can make a Quechua grievance legible to a Spanish bench. Everything he will later denounce he first learns as an employee, in the room, holding the words as they pass from one side to the other.
suggested_refs: The office of the Abogado General de los Indios in the viceroyalty of Peru
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guamán Poma de Ayala'

stops.name: Huamanga, at the elbow of Fray Martín de Murúa
stops.date_confidence: attested as a working relationship in the late 1580s or early 1590s; the year is a midpoint, and the direction of borrowing between the two manuscripts remains contested in the scholarship
stops.campa: The Mercedarian friar Martín de Murúa is writing a history of the Incas, and Guamán Poma works at his side, gathering material for him and drawing for him. Images and text pass between the two manuscripts in a traffic scholars still cannot fully sort, and the two men fall out. The chronicle will later show a friar named Murúa beating an indigenous weaver; whether that drawing is portrait or revenge is settled by no source. Guamán Poma has now watched a book about the Andes being assembled by a Spaniard out of Andean material.
suggested_refs: The Galvin and Getty manuscripts of Murúa's Historia general del Piru, and their shared hands
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'
Rolena Adorno and Ivan Boserup, studies on the Guamán Poma and Murúa relationship

stops.name: Huamanga, taken into Pérez de Gamboa's retinue
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1587 in the Spanish account, which names Juan Pérez de Gamboa as corregidor of Huancavelica and afterward visitador; the itinerary sometimes attached to this commission, Cuzco and Huamanga, is not supported by that source and is not carried here
stops.campa: Juan Pérez de Gamboa, corregidor of Huancavelica and afterward visitador, takes Guamán Poma into his retinue for the inspection circuit. The Spanish account gives the year and the man and not the road; the towns commonly attached to this commission are inference and are left as inference. What the commission does is fixed enough: it rides into a province, counts the tributaries, hears the complaints, and rides out. He is inside the machinery of colonial government with a notebook, and it is not the notebook his employers are keeping.
suggested_refs: The visita records of Juan Pérez de Gamboa, 1587
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guamán Poma de Ayala'
Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)

stops.name: Santa Bárbara, the mercury under Huancavelica
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1588: the Spanish account records the inspection of the Huancavelica mines under Pedro de Arteaga Mendiola and gives him no title, so the description of him as an oidor is dropped; the coordinate is the Santa Bárbara mining settlement rather than the city
stops.campa: Pedro de Arteaga Mendiola inspects the mercury workings at Santa Bárbara above Huancavelica, and Guamán Poma goes as translator. Mercury amalgamates the silver of Potosí, and the mita sends indigenous men into these galleries in rotation, where the vapor takes them. The chronicle will describe men who go down and do not come up, and the passage carries the flat authority of a man who stood at the mouth of the shaft with a Spanish official's questions in his mouth. He is a quarter century from writing it down.
suggested_refs: The Santa Bárbara mercury mine above Huancavelica, the mina de la muerte
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guamán Poma de Ayala'
Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986), ch. 2
GeoNames, Santa Bárbara, Huancavelica

stops.name: Castrovirreyna, the silver camps
stops.date_confidence: attested as part of the inspection service in the 1590s; the year is a midpoint and no document fixes a month or a specific camp
stops.campa: The circuit crosses into the silver camps of Castrovirreyna, high and cold, where the mita quota must be filled from villages that still have to find men for their own fields. He is recording, on someone else's commission, the material for an indictment nobody has commissioned. Far to the east, in the country Hernando Arias de Saavedra governs, the same two instruments are named as the pair by which the conquerors abused the Indians: the mita and the encomienda. The instruments are viceregal. Only the altitude changes.
suggested_refs: The colonial silver workings of Castrovirreyna and their mita quotas
sources: Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)
Franklin Pease, Guamán Poma y su crónica (1980)
hernando_arias_de_saavedra.journey.json

stops.name: Huaytará, the church on the Inca wall
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the stop is read off the inspection route through the colonial Castrovirreyna corregimiento, with no document naming Guamán Poma here; Huaytará is today the seat of its own province, created in 1984
stops.campa: At Huaytará the parish church stands on Inca wall, colonial masonry set directly upon fitted stone that no mortar holds. The town lies in the corregimiento of Castrovirreyna, on the road down toward the coast. The superimposition is the argument of his book in one building: Christian authority raised on Inca foundations it did not lay and cannot match in the joint. He will draw dozens of towns this way, church and ushnu inside one frame, and leave the reader to see which of the two is plumb.
suggested_refs: The church of San Juan Bautista at Huaytará, built on an Inca structure
sources: Regional geography of the Castrovirreyna inspection route
GeoNames, Huaytará

segments.name: The Circuit of the Inca Roads

stops.name: Cusco, the navel of the world
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Cusco chapters read as direct observation and the inspection circuit passes through, but no notarial record places him in the city on any day; the pin is the canonical atlas Cusco, inherited unchanged
stops.campa: He passes through Qosqo, the navel of the world, where Francisco Pizarro rode into Huacaypata sixty years before. The streets run over palace foundations and the cathedral rises on Inca stone. His drawings of the plaza, the four quarters and the succession of the Incas suggest a man who has stood here and looked, though no notarial paper puts him in the city on any given day. He will place Cusco at the center of a world map on which Castile is a province at the edge, and he will not be joking.
suggested_refs: The Nueva corónica's mapa mundi del reino de las Indias, with Cusco at the center
sources: pizarro.journey.json
bolivar.journey.json
micaela_bastidas.journey.json
Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)
Nueva corónica, Cusco chapters, poma.kb.dk

stops.name: Vitcos, the house of the last Incas
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Pérez de Gamboa circuit covers Vilcabamba; the month is nominal, and the fall of the neo-Inca state at Vitcos and Vilcabamba in June 1572 is separately attested
stops.campa: On the ridge between Huancacalle and Pucyura stands Vitcos, the house of the last Incas, who held Vilcabamba for thirty-six years after Cajamarca and lost it in 1572, when Túpac Amaru was taken and beheaded in the plaza at Cusco. The inspection circuit that employs Guamán Poma covers this province. He gathers the account of the resistance from men who were alive for it, and his chronicle will name the last Incas in order, as legitimate, as a line ended by an execution rather than by a conquest.
suggested_refs: The ridge site of Vitcos above Huancacalle, Vilcabamba district, La Convención
sources: Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)
Franklin Pease on the Pérez de Gamboa commission
English Wikipedia, 'Vitcos'

stops.name: Andahuaylas, the road between the cities
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from route geography alone: no document isolates his presence at Andahuaylas from the wider itinerary, and the date is nominal
stops.campa: The road between Huamanga and Cusco drops into the Chanka valley of Andahuaylas, a waystation for the Inca and for the Spanish after them. No paper isolates his presence here; the stop is read off the route, because a man traveling that circuit passes through. The chronicle's chapters on the Inca road, the tambos stocked at intervals, the chaski runners in relay, are the chapters of someone who has used that road as an official and knows how much of it still works and how much has been let go.
suggested_refs: The Inca road and tambo system between Huamanga and Cusco
sources: Rolena Adorno on the Pérez de Gamboa inspection
Nueva corónica, chapters on Inca administration, poma.kb.dk

stops.name: Jauja, the valley of the Wanka lords
stops.date_confidence: attested as part of the inspection itinerary in the 1590s; the year is a midpoint within that service
stops.campa: In the Mantaro valley the Wanka lords hold Jauja, which the Inca made an administrative hub and which the Spanish briefly considered for their capital before choosing the coast. Guamán Poma comes with the inspection and takes down grievances that read as testimony heard rather than copied. The Wanka fought beside the Spanish against the Inca and were rewarded as everyone else was rewarded. He is assembling, province by province, a survey of who was promised what and of what actually arrived.
suggested_refs: Hatun Xauxa, Inca administrative center of the Mantaro valley
sources: Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)
Franklin Pease, Guamán Poma y su crónica (1980)

stops.name: Vilcashuamán, the ushnu on the royal road
stops.date_confidence: undated: the site falls within the Huamanga jurisdiction he serves for years, but no document fixes a visit and the date here is nominal
stops.campa: Vilcashuamán, the Inca waystation on the road from Cusco to the sea, keeps its ushnu, the stepped platform where the Inca sat above an assembled province. It lies within the Huamanga jurisdiction he serves for years as interpreter and witness. No document fixes a visit. His account of the ushnu's use and of the ordering of the roads is the account of a man for whom these are not ruins; in the chronicle the Inca administration is drawn as a working system, described in the present tense of a state that functions.
suggested_refs: The ushnu and Temple of the Sun at Vilcashuamán
sources: Nueva corónica, chapters on Inca administration, poma.kb.dk
Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)

stops.name: Huamanga, working the composición de tierras
stops.date_confidence: attested to around 1594 in the English account, which names a Spanish land judge at Huamanga without giving the officer's name
stops.campa: A Spanish judge at Huamanga hires him for the composición de tierras, the proceedings by which colonial title to land is fixed and unfixed. He works in the papers: boundaries, claims, the documents that make a holding lawful. He is perhaps sixty years old, and he now knows exactly how a land title is made in this jurisdiction, who signs it, what it costs, and what a claim must contain to survive a hearing. He has spent his working life preparing, without meaning to, for the suit he is about to file in his own name.
suggested_refs: The composición de tierras proceedings of the Huamanga corregimiento
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'
Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)

stops.name: Valle de Chupas, the suit for the cacicazgo
stops.date_confidence: attested that the suits fall in the late 1590s and fail; the coordinate is the Chupas area in Chiara district south of Ayacucho, and a reducción named Concepción de Chupas is unverified in the gazetteers and is not asserted here
stops.campa: In the valley of Chupas, south of Huamanga, he sues to recover the cacicazgo and the lands, asserting hereditary right through his father's line and his mother's. The valley already carries a Spanish memory: in September 1542 Vaca de Castro broke Diego de Almagro the younger on this ground, conquerors killing conquerors over the spoil. Guamán Poma's battle is fought in ink, before a colonial bench, with the genealogy he has spent his life asserting entered as evidence. The genealogy is the only property he has.
suggested_refs: The Chupas battlefield of 16 September 1542, Chiara district, Huamanga
sources: Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)
Guillermo Lohmann Villena on colonial land litigation in Huamanga
Spanish Wikipedia, 'Batalla de Chupas'
GeoNames, Chupas, Chiara

stops.name: Huamanga, the corregidor's court rules
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1600 in both the English and Spanish accounts, which agree on the loss and the stripping of property; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: The court rules against him. He loses the lands, the cacicazgo, the title, and by his own account everything else he owns; the corregidor strips him of the honors he has spent decades documenting. The man who spent thirty years inside the apparatus, interpreting for visitadores and drafting for land judges, learns what the apparatus does when he stands in front of it as a claimant with an Andean name and a lineage no notary ever wrote down. From this ruling forward he has no household of his own.
stops.quote: O gran senor de los senores, misericordioso Dios! O Dios todopoderoso que teneys piedad y misericordia con tus pobres de los hombres de las dichas ciudades y uillas, aldeas deste rreyno!
stops.quote_source: Nueva corónica y buen gobierno, prologue to Christian readers (f. 1085), transcription at poma.kb.dk
suggested_refs: The surviving Huamanga land-litigation papers of the Chupas suit
sources: Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)
English and Spanish Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'

stops.name: Huamanga, the plaza mayor and the banishment
stops.date_confidence: the banishment is attested on every side; the month is nominal, and the public flogging that popular syntheses add, at two hundred lashes, travels without a primary citation and is not resolved here
stops.campa: He is banished from Huamanga. Some accounts add a public flogging of two hundred lashes, but the number travels without a primary citation and the sources disagree over whether any flogging took place; the banishment itself is attested everywhere. He walks out of the city at something past sixty, propertyless, carrying a lineage no court will recognize. Behind him the bells ring the hours of a jurisdiction that has just written him out of its own records, in a city he had served as its interpreter.
stops.quote: os hazeys otra Sodoma, auariento enemigo de los pobres de Jesucristo
stops.quote_source: Nueva corónica y buen gobierno, prologue to Christian readers of the towns of Indians (f. 1085), transcription at poma.kb.dk
suggested_refs: The plaza mayor of Huamanga, now Ayacucho, and its colonial cathedral
sources: Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)
English and Spanish Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'

stops.name: Sondondo, the return that no paper records
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from tradition and from the manuscript's affectionate treatment of the valley; no document places him in Suntuntu after the exiles begin, and the manuscript names no writing place at all
stops.campa: Tradition brings him back to the valley of his birth in these years, drafting the earliest sections of the chronicle among the terraces. The manuscript names no writing place, and its author describes himself as constantly walking; no document puts him in Suntuntu once the exiles begin. The return is inferred from the shape of a life and from the loving detail in which the Sondondo towns are drawn: Cabana, Andamarca, the irrigated steps of the valley, the province he keeps calling his own even after it has stopped being his.
stops.quote: para sacar en linpio estas dichas historias ube tanto trabajo por ser cin escrito ni letra alguna, cino no mas de quipos [cordeles con nudos] y rrelaciones de muchas lenguaxes
stops.quote_source: Nueva corónica y buen gobierno, Prologue to the Christian Reader (f. 11), transcription at poma.kb.dk
suggested_refs: The drawings of the Sondondo valley towns in the Nueva corónica
sources: Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)
Royal Danish Library, poma.kb.dk

stops.name: Lucanas, the second exile
stops.date_confidence: sources disagree: 1606 in the Spanish account, 1608 in other circulating scholarship, with no reconciliation; the corregidor of Lucanas as the ordering officer is attested
stops.campa: The corregidor of Lucanas, his own home province, exiles him a second time. Sources give the year as 1606 or as 1608 and do not reconcile. He is old now, without property, and the road has become the only fixed condition of his life. Both banishments follow one sequence: he asserts a right, he documents the right, and an official removes him from the district in which that right would have to be recognized. The chronicle is composed by a man who is being moved along.
suggested_refs: The colonial corregimiento of Lucanas and its provincial seat
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guamán Poma de Ayala'
Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)

stops.name: Huamanga region, the itinerant years
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline for roughly 1600 to 1615 from internal evidence and the manuscript's own account of how the book was made; no year within that span can be fixed to a place
stops.campa: For more than a decade he walks the towns of the corregimiento that once employed him, with no settled residence, composing. Nearly twelve hundred pages accumulate, some four hundred of them full-page drawings, in an orthography nobody is correcting and a Spanish nobody taught him formally. He is writing to Philip III of Spain, unasked, on the authority of what he has seen. The conditions of the writing are the conditions the book protests: dispossession, exile, a man with no address addressing a king.
stops.quote: no ser letrado ni dotor ni lesenciado ni latino
stops.quote_source: Nueva corónica y buen gobierno, Letter to King Philip III (ff. 8-9), transcription at poma.kb.dk
suggested_refs: The chapter on how the author was able to write this book, poma.kb.dk pp. 916-921
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'
Royal Danish Library, poma.kb.dk, pp. 916-921
Rolena Adorno, Writing and Resistance (1986)

stops.name: Huarochirí, the trials of Francisco de Ávila
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the denunciation of Ávila is in the manuscript, but whether the knowledge comes from travel or from informants inside the same extirpation networks is undetermined, and the date is a midpoint of Ávila's campaign
stops.campa: He denounces the idolatry trials that Francisco de Ávila conducts in Huarochirí, the province on the inland road toward Lima, and the sharpness of the denunciation reads to scholars as knowledge got at first hand or from informants inside the same extirpation networks that once employed him under Albornoz. Out of Ávila's own campaign comes the Huarochirí manuscript, the great book of Andean myth set down in Quechua. Two books are being made out of the same machinery, from opposite ends of it.
suggested_refs: The Huarochirí Manuscript, compiled under Ávila's extirpation campaign
sources: Rolena Adorno on Guamán Poma's critique of Ávila
Frank Salomon, scholarship on the Huarochirí Manuscript
English Wikipedia, 'Huarochirí'

stops.name: Huamanga, the last page of the corónica
stops.date_confidence: the final composition date is usually placed at 1615, though the closing date has been read by some scholars as 1616 and the Royal Danish Library catalogues the work as 1615/1616; page counts are given as 1,189 or 1,180, with 397 or 398 drawings
stops.campa: The last page carries the royal arms of Castile and a Latin motto beneath them. The work is titled El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno, near eleven hundred and ninety pages, close to four hundred drawings, addressed to the king of Spain. Its final date is read as 1615, and by some scholars as 1616. Nothing in it was commissioned, paid for or requested. It is the only history of the conquest written by an Andean and addressed directly to the sovereign in whose name the conquest was carried out.
stops.quote: PRIMER nueua coronica y buen gobierno deste rreyno. El dicho libro conpuesto y entitulado por don Phelipe Guaman Poma de Ayala.
stops.quote_source: Nueva corónica y buen gobierno, title page (f. 1), MS GKS 2232 4to, transcription at poma.kb.dk
suggested_refs: Drawing 398, the royal arms on the manuscript's closing page, poma.kb.dk f. 1189
sources: Royal Danish Library, poma.kb.dk, manuscript description
English Wikipedia, 'El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno'

stops.name: Camino real, the walk down to Lima
stops.date_confidence: the journey is narrated in the manuscript as chapter 36, pp. 1104-1139, and follows the completed book, so it is placed after the closing date of 1615 rather than at the 1613 carried earlier; whether it records a literal itinerary or closes the book's argument is debated, no notarial trace confirms the towns, and this pin is an arbitrary route marker
stops.campa: He sets out on the royal road toward Lima, the road the Inca built and the Spanish inherited, an old man carrying a letter nobody asked him to write, his son Francisco walking with him. Chapter thirty-six of the manuscript narrates the journey to the City of Kings. Whether it is an itinerary or the closing argument of the book, staged, is debated; no notarial trace confirms a single town. The drawing shows two figures, the dogs, the baggage, moving downhill in winter.
stops.quote: CAMINA EL AVTOR con su hijo don Francisco de Ayala. Sale de la prouincia a la ciudad de los Reys de Lima a dar quenta a su Magestad. Y sale pobre, desnudo y camina enbierno.
stops.quote_source: Nueva corónica y buen gobierno, caption to Drawing 385 (f. 1105), transcription at poma.kb.dk
suggested_refs: Drawing 385, the author and his son on the road to Lima, poma.kb.dk f. 1105
sources: Royal Danish Library, poma.kb.dk, ch. 36, pp. 1104-1139

stops.name: Lima, the City of Kings
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the arrival rests on the chronicle's own account of the journey, with no Lima notarial or viceregal record placing him in the city; the month is nominal and the pin is the canonical atlas Lima, inherited unchanged
stops.campa: He comes down into the City of Kings, which Francisco Pizarro founded in 1535 on the valley the Inca called Rímac, looking for a channel by which a manuscript might reach a king. There is no record of an audience with the viceroy, no receipt, no acknowledgment of any kind. The inference that he reached Lima at all rests on the book's own account of the road. Somewhere in this city the largest object ever made by an Andean hand for Spanish eyes leaves that hand, and no paper says into whose.

stops.name: Cercado de Lima, the walled parish
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no document places him in the Cercado; the parish is named as the plausible lodging for an indigenous arrival in Lima, and the date is nominal
stops.campa: If he is in Lima at all, the Cercado is where an indigenous man lodges: the walled parish the Jesuits administer for native residents, outside the Spanish traza, with its own gate and its own curfew. No document places him there. It is named here as the likely landing of an old man arriving in a city laid out with no room for him, where the parish for people like him is a compound with a wall around it. His book has a chapter on the ordering of cities. The ordering, here, is a wall and a curfew.
suggested_refs: El Cercado, the Jesuit-administered indigenous parish of colonial Lima

stops.name: Lima, death without a record
stops.date_confidence: direct contradiction left open: the English account gives after 1616 at Lima, the Spanish account gives 1615 at Lima; that he died in Lima at all is itself an inference, since no burial, parish or notarial record has been located
stops.campa: He dies in or near Lima. No burial entry or parish register fixes the day or the ground, and that he died in Lima at all is inference. The English account says after 1616; the Spanish account says 1615, the year it assumes the book was finished. Neither offers a grave. No tomb or marker is recorded in the archives searched, and no source says a tomb was destroyed. Nothing was lost here, because the register was never kept. The last dated thing he leaves behind is a page number in a book nobody has read.
suggested_refs: The absent burial record: no parish entry for Guamán Poma has been located in any archive

stops.name: Lima, the crossing nobody logged
stops.date_confidence: explicit evidentiary gap: nothing documents how the manuscript left Peru, and the span between the author's death and the first named European owner runs to roughly half a century; the date here only marks the opening of that gap
stops.campa: How eleven hundred pages leave Peru, cross the Atlantic and enter a European collection is recorded nowhere. No shipping manifest survives, and no ecclesiastical correspondence. Philip III never receives the book, and no evidence suggests he ever heard of it. Between the author's death and the manuscript's first named European owner lies half a century of silence, which the object comes through intact. The object is kept and catalogued. The grave of the man who made it is not recorded at all.
suggested_refs: The undocumented transit of GKS 2232 4to from Peru to northern Europe, 1616 to 1662

stops.name: Copenhagen, the book in a Danish collection
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, not attestation: the Olivares-to-Lerche route is called speculation by the sources that carry it, the 1662 inventory is not documented, and the Danish record of Cornelius Pedersen Lerche mentions no such book; only the manuscript's later presence in the royal collection is firm
stops.campa: The manuscript surfaces in Denmark. One account has it passing through the library of the Count-Duke of Olivares in Spain and being sold to Cornelius Pedersen Lerche, Danish envoy to the Spanish court until 1662, but the sources that carry this route call it speculation, and the Danish record of Lerche mentions no such book. It enters the royal collection and is catalogued GKS 2232 4to. For two and a half centuries nobody opens it who can read what it is.

stops.name: The southern sierra, the rising of 1780
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1780-1781 as carried in micaela_bastidas.journey.json; the pin and the dating follow that file
stops.campa: A cacique claiming descent from the Inca rises in the southern sierra, and Micaela Bastidas writes the letters that carry the rising to caciques across the provinces: the mita drafts out of Canas y Canchis, the same grievance, the same network of curacas, the same country. They are executed in the plaza of Cusco in 1781, and Areche's sentence then bans Inca names, Inca dress and the keeping of Inca genealogies. Guamán Poma had petitioned a king with exactly such a genealogy, and the petition had not arrived.
suggested_refs: Areche's 1781 sentencia banning Inca names, dress and genealogies
sources: micaela_bastidas.journey.json

stops.name: Cusco, the decree two centuries late
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1825 in bolivar.journey.json, which places the entry into Cuzco and the order abolishing cacique tributes in that year without fixing month or day here
stops.campa: Simón Bolívar enters Cusco under arches raised in the Inca manner and writes from that city an order abolishing the cacique tributes. The reform arrives two hundred and ten years after an old man walked down to Lima to ask a king for it, and it arrives from a republic rather than a crown. The manuscript that asked is in Copenhagen, catalogued, unread, in a library belonging to a kingdom that had no part in Peru and no reader who could follow its Spanish or its Quechua.
suggested_refs: Bolívar's 1825 decrees from Cuzco on indigenous tribute and cacique authority
sources: bolivar.journey.json

stops.name: Copenhagen, Pietschmann opens the book
stops.date_confidence: sources disagree on the year: the English account dates the rediscovery to 1908, the Spanish account to 1907, and neither concedes the other; the identification by Richard Pietschmann in the Danish royal collection is attested on both sides
stops.campa: The German scholar Richard Pietschmann identifies the manuscript in the Danish royal collection and announces it to European and American scholarship. The English account dates the find to 1908, the Spanish account to 1907; neither concedes the other. Three centuries end in a reading room. The only history of the conquest written by an Andean and addressed to the king who ordered it had been sitting in a foreign library, whole and catalogued and unread, for longer than the viceroyalty had lasted.
suggested_refs: Pietschmann's 1908 announcement of the Guamán Poma manuscript to European scholarship
sources: English and Spanish Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'

stops.name: Paris, the first facsimile
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1936: Paul Rivet's Paris facsimile, described in the sources as heavily retouched
stops.campa: Paul Rivet publishes the first facsimile edition in Paris, heavily retouched, the drawings cleaned up by hands that believed they were helping. It is the first time the book can be held by anyone not admitted to Copenhagen. Retouched or not, the four hundred drawings enter the world: the quipucamayoc with his cords, the mine gallery, the priest with his stick, the mother hiding her child from the corregidor, the author walking with his son and his dogs on the road down to Lima in winter. The argument he made in pictures begins to be read by people who cannot read his Spanish.
suggested_refs: Paul Rivet's 1936 Paris facsimile edition of the Nueva corónica
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'

stops.name: Copenhagen, the letter delivered late
stops.date_confidence: the Murra and Adorno critical transcription is attested to 1980; the launch year of the Royal Danish Library digital facsimile is contradictory, given as 2001 by the English account and 2011 by the Spanish, and the site itself does not state it in the sections retrieved
stops.campa: John Murra and Rolena Adorno, with Jorge Urioste, publish the critical transcription made from the original itself, and it becomes the standard edition. The Royal Danish Library later puts the whole manuscript online with Adorno as editor; the English account dates that facsimile to 2001, the Spanish to 2011. The letter reaches the subjects of its addressee four centuries late, page by page, free of charge, in the orthography its author actually used, which the editors decline to correct.
suggested_refs: Murra, Adorno and Urioste, critical edition of 1980; the digital facsimile at poma.kb.dk
sources: English and Spanish Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'
Royal Danish Library, poma.kb.dk

stops.name: Madrid, the pages taken into paint
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1992: the Madrid showing of Herman Braun-Vega's series appropriating pages of the Nueva corónica
stops.campa: The Peruvian-French painter Herman Braun-Vega takes pages of the chronicle into a series of canvases on colonial violence and the evangelizing Church, shown in Madrid in the quincentenary year, in the capital of the crown the letter was addressed to. The drawings work on a gallery wall as they worked on the page, as an argument made in pictures. The unschooled Spanish they were bound to reached no reader in his lifetime. The pictures hang four centuries late in the city he was writing to.
suggested_refs: Herman Braun-Vega's 1992 Madrid retrospective and its Guamán Poma appropriations
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala'

stops.name: Cusco, the name and the cords
stops.date_confidence: undated: the Centro Guamán Poma de Ayala's founding year is not stated on its own site, and the date here is nominal; the Bolivian literary prize in his name is likewise undated in the sources consulted
stops.campa: In Cusco an organization carries his name into present institutional life, working on governance, civic participation and schooling, and its own website gives no account of why the name was chosen. Bolivia awards a Premio Guamán Poma de Ayala for narrative written in indigenous languages. No statue of him is documented anywhere. The cords he drew the quipucamayocs reading are taken up again by Cecilia Vicuña, who knots them in wool and names the burning of the quipus for what it was.
suggested_refs: The Centro Guamán Poma de Ayala, Jirón Retiro 346, Cusco

stops.name: Sondondo, the falcon still expected
stops.date_confidence: tradition, undated: an Andean oral tradition reported in the sources as legend rather than history, with no date attached; the year here is nominal and the pin returns to the valley of his birth
stops.campa: An Andean tradition holds that his descendants are kept and hidden, protected against a day when the Peruvian empire is retaken, and it carries a prophecy of a hawk that will fly high where the sun surrenders. The sources report it as legend and not as history. In the valley of Sondondo the terraces still hold the hillsides, cut in steps by people who kept their accounts on knotted cord, and the man who drew those cords for a king has no grave, no portrait and no recorded date of birth.
suggested_refs: The Andean oral tradition of the hidden descendants and the hawk prophecy
